chunks: "I'd use one N-channel FET, like a BSS138. The gate goes to the low-voltage rail, say 3. 3 volts. The source connects to the 3.
3 volts side signal, the drain to the 5 volts side signal, and each side gets its own pull-up resistor to its own rail, around 4. 7 kilohms to 10 kilohms. It works in three cases.
When nobody is pulling low, both sides are high, the source is at 3. 3 volts, the gate is at 3. 3 volts, so Vgs is zero and the FET is off. The 3. 3 volts side sits at 3.
3 volts and the 5 volts side sits at 5 volts. If the low-voltage device pulls its line low, the source drops to about zero, Vgs becomes 3.
3 volts, the FET turns on, and it pulls the 5 volts side low too. If the 5 volts device pulls low, the drain falls, but the FET is off at first.
The body diode conducts from source to drain, pulling the source down to about 0. 6 volts. Now Vgs is about 2.
7 volts, so the FET turns on and pulls the source the rest of the way to the low level.
So either side can pull the line low and the other follows, while each high stays at its own rail. It only works for open-drain signals, not for strongly driven push-pull ones."
